title: Stratification
body:
Split the data so that **every part has the same class proportions as the whole.** If 10% of the
full set is class 1, then 10% of the training set and 10% of the test set are class 1, by
construction rather than by luck.

It is [[STATISTICS]]'s stratified sampling applied to a train/test split: divide the population
into strata (here, the classes), then sample within each stratum instead of from the pool. Statistics owns the general method; this note is the [[Classification]] use of it.

## Why a plain random split is not good enough

A random split gets the proportions right *on average*, and the variance around that average is
what hurts. Two cases where it bites:

- **Rare classes.** With 20 positives in 2000 examples and an 80/20 split, the test set gets 4
  positives in expectation, and getting 0 or 1 by chance is entirely plausible. [[Sensitivity]] is
  then computed from a handful of cases, or is undefined, and the measurement is noise.
- **Small test sets.** The fewer examples, the larger the proportional swing, so exactly when you
  can least afford a skewed split you are most likely to get one.

Stratifying removes that variance rather than reducing it. The proportions are exact, so the test
set is measuring the model instead of measuring the draw.

## What it does not fix

**It is not a cure for class imbalance**, and the two get confused. Stratification preserves the
imbalance faithfully into every split, which is the right thing to do: the test set should look
like reality. Fixing the imbalance itself is a different set of tools (resampling, class weights in
the [[Loss Function]]), applied to the training set only, never to the test set.

It also does not make accuracy a usable metric. That is still [[Sensitivity]], [[Specificity]], and
precision's job, for the reason in [[True Negative]].

The same idea generalises to cross-validation, where every fold is stratified, and it is why
`train_test_split(..., stratify=y)` exists in the [[NumPy]]-adjacent tooling.

## Related

- [[Classification]], [[Binary Classification]]: what is being split
- [[Confusion Matrix]], [[Sensitivity]], [[Specificity]]: the measurements it protects
- [[Sampling Distribution]] ([[STATISTICS]]): the variance argument
- [[Bias]]: what a skewed split introduces
